extracted.intended_audience: general public; public-health reformers, physicians, architects, factory/prison/ship owners and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive hygienic and design principles for dwellings, workplaces, schools, prisons, and ships to prevent pulmonary disease (especially consumption/tuberculosis) through ventilation, exposure to open air, and reduction of airborne contaminants. Includes medical, architectural, occupational, and ethical recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-air exposure as primary remedy and prevention for pulmonary disease
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is a cure for consumption ... Even in its advanced stages the disease may be arrested by roughing it — I mean by adopting savage habits, and living out-doors altogether, and in all kinds of weather.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendation to send consumptives and those with respiratory complaints outdoors (examples: driving patients into woods, sending to Minnesota/Northern Michigan or Florida depending on physician). Asserts low outdoor temperature does not injure lungs and dry cold preserves tissue; cites populations (Norwegians, Icelanders, Yakuts, inhabitants of Senegal highlands) as evidence of low tuberculosis rates in cold, open-air climates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent and avoid the 'troglodyte-habit' (habitual indoor life)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The great principal curse of the troglodyte-habit is its influence on the respiratory organs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat habitual indoor confinement as a primary cause of pulmonary disease and other ills; encourage outdoor life and oppose customs/ethics that valorize seclusion (e.g., monastic celibacy, closed convent-schools). Notes children’s instinctive preference for fresh air as evidence of natural corrective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buildings must admit fresh air as well as light (architectural ventilation requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If ever we recognize a truth ... that our noses were given us for some practical purpose, the architecture of our dwellings, our factories, school-rooms, and places of worship, will be speedily corrected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates architectural design that ensures liberal apertures/windows that admit both light and fresh air (criticizes glass obstructing ventilation). Applies to private dwellings, factories, schools, places of worship, and immigrant steerage. Example anti-patterns: closed windows, overheated rooms, 'floating Black Hole of Calcutta' steerage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rebreathed, azotized, or carbon-saturated indoor atmospheres
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The deleterious consequences ... of breathing the same air over and over again arise ... from the circumstance that the confined atmosphere may become azotized or surcharged with carbon to the limit of its absorbing powers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle that repeated inhalation of exhausted air depletes oxygen and increases harmful gases; likens reinspiring used air to 'a famished animal devouring its own feces.' Implies need for ventilation rates sufficient to prevent accumulation of CO2, carbon, and azotic changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent airborne particulates and industrial effluvia in workplaces
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Working-men employed in localities whose azotized atmosphere is loaded besides with particles of flying cotton-fibre, metallic dust, or fatty vapors, inspire substances which are just as indigestible to their lungs ... and like these cause a rapid deterioration of the tissues.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workplaces (factories, mills) must control airborne fibers, metallic dust, and vapors—these are directly injurious to lung tissue and predispose to consumption. Encourages ventilation and removal of such contaminants; identifies factory districts as having higher consumption mortality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical/epidemiological link: indoor occupations increase consumption deaths
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Our home statistics show that the percentage of deaths by consumption in each State bears an exact proportion to the greater or smaller number of inhabitants who follow in-door occupations, and is highest in the factory districts ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mortality statistics and comparisons (e.g., Glasgow vs. northern pastoral regions) to evaluate risk; monitor rates by occupation/geography as an indicator of indoor-air harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schoolrooms and child health: provide openings and fresh air
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote: child securing a seat by a knot-hole 'imbibed comfort and inspiration ... from a flask' and the author argues children’s repugnance to closed air suggests school design should allow fresh-air access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design schoolrooms with apertures/ventilation appropriate for children’s physiological needs; recognize children’s instinctive preference for fresh air as evidence against overclose schooling. Anti-pattern: overcrowded, unventilated classrooms that 'inoculate' children with seeds of disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prisons and punishment should not use unhealthy air as punitive measure
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Our right to diet our criminals on the ineffable mixture of odors which they are now obliged to accept as air depends on the settlement of the question whether the object of punishment is reform or revenge?... In the first case there is no more excuse for saturating the lungs of a prisoner with the seeds of tuberculosis than there would be for feeding him on trichinae or inoculating him with the leprosy-virus.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical/administrative standard: prisons should not expose inmates to miasmatic, poorly ventilated air as punishment—if objective is reform, humane, health-preserving conditions are required. Calls for redesign of prisons to admit fresh air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ship steerage and immigrant transport must be ventilated
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Even the builder of an immigrant-ship will find a way to modify that floating Black Hole of Calcutta called the steerage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates redesigning steerage spaces to allow fresh air and prevent miasmatic conditions that produce rapid onset of consumption in newly confined individuals (examples: slave-trader steerage causing disease in African captives).

rubrics_metrics.name: Employers and public duties: do not expose workers to known health hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: miners left a colliery en masse because owner shirked duty of providing safety-lamps; navvies left when food adulterated; slave-owners tested 'wind' of imported slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers have an obligation to provide safe working conditions (ventilation, safety-lamps, unadulterated provisions). Worker resistance to health hazards is a social corrective; policymakers should enforce employer duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiration is a primary and frequent physiological need—design accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The difference is made up by the labors of the upper or pectoral department, which renews its supply of raw material independently ... twenty times per minute, or 70,000 times in twenty-four hours! With every breath we draw we take into our lungs about one pint of air ... the quantity ... in a day to 675 cubic feet.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative physiological claim to justify ventilation standards: because respiration is continuous and large in volume, indoor air quality must meet high standards—design ventilation systems to supply sufficient fresh air per person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake cold outdoor air as harmful to lungs
rubrics_metrics.description: 'That low temperature in open air does not injure our lungs has been recognized even by old-school physicians ...'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject common anti-pattern belief that cold outdoor air causes pectoral complaints; instead point to artificial overheated atmospheres indoors as the cause. Supports policies favoring outdoor exposure even in low temperatures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural instincts and education: prefer correcting perverse cultural practices
rubrics_metrics.description: 'To whatever is really beneficent we are commonly drawn by natural attraction, and whatever appears violently repulsive to youthful minds may be justly suspected of containing more of evil than of good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health interventions should align with natural instincts (children's desire for fresh air) and counter cultural/ethical teachings that denigrate natural outdoor life. Educational reform to restore appreciation of outdoor life and correct unhealthy customs is recommended.
